Riverton officials lifted a three-day boil-water advisory on Friday after laboratory tests confirmed that the town’s drinking water met safety standards. The advisory affected approximately 18,000 residents following an equipment failure at the municipal treatment plant.

The problem began early Tuesday when a control valve stopped working during routine maintenance. Pressure dropped across several neighborhoods, creating a risk that untreated groundwater could enter damaged sections of the distribution network. Officials said they had not confirmed that contamination actually occurred.

Residents were instructed to boil tap water before drinking it, preparing food, brushing their teeth, or making ice. Water could still be used for laundry and most cleaning activities. The town distributed bottled water at two community centers, prioritizing older residents and households without transportation.

Plant manager Elena Torres said technicians replaced the failed valve Tuesday afternoon, but repairs alone were insufficient to lift the advisory. Workers also flushed affected pipes and collected samples from twelve locations across the network.

“We needed evidence that the water was safe throughout the system, rather than simply evidence that the broken equipment had been repaired,” Torres said.

Two consecutive rounds of testing found no harmful bacteria. The second round was completed late Thursday, and the county health department authorized the town to lift the advisory Friday morning.

Riverton General Hospital continued operating throughout the disruption using stored drinking water and temporary supplies. Two primary schools closed Wednesday because they lacked enough bottled water for meals and drinking stations. Both reopened Thursday after deliveries arrived.

The town estimated the immediate response cost at $86,000, including repairs, laboratory testing, bottled water, and overtime. Finance director Samuel Reed said the money would initially come from an existing emergency reserve. No increase in household water charges has been approved.

Some residents criticized the timing of the first public warning. The pressure failure was detected at 5:40 a.m. Tuesday, but the advisory was not issued until 8:15 a.m. Mayor Priya Shah said an internal review would examine that delay and whether automated alerts could be sent sooner.

The mayor emphasized that the review would be separate from a proposed modernization project for the treatment plant. That project, estimated at $3.2 million, has not received funding or final council approval.

Independent engineer Daniel Wu, who inspected the repaired equipment, said the failed valve showed signs of wear but that a complete investigation was needed before assigning responsibility. He cautioned against concluding that the entire treatment plant was unsafe because one component had failed.

Residents have been advised to run cold taps for five minutes and discard ice made during the advisory. Restaurants must also clean equipment connected to the water supply before resuming normal use.

Officials said no illnesses had been linked to the incident as of Friday afternoon. The town plans to publish its emergency communication review within thirty days and hold a public meeting the following week.
